verses.text: Brothers, I couldn’t speak to you as to spiritual, but as to fleshly, as to babies in Christ.
I fed you with milk, not with meat; for you weren’t yet ready. Indeed, not even now are you ready,
for you are still fleshly. For insofar as there is jealousy, strife, and factions among you, aren’t you fleshly, and don’t you walk in the ways of men?
For when one says, “I follow Paul,” and another, “I follow Apollos,” aren’t you fleshly?
Who then is Apollos, and who is Paul, but servants through whom you believed; and each as the Lord gave to him?
I planted. Apollos watered. But God gave the increase.
So then neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase.
Now he who plants and he who waters are the same, but each will receive his own reward according to his own labor.
For we are God’s fellow workers. You are God’s farming, God’s building.
According to the grace of God which was given to me, as a wise master builder I laid a foundation, and another builds on it. But let each man be careful how he builds on it.
For no one can lay any other foundation than that which has been laid, which is Jesus Christ.
But if anyone builds on the foundation with gold, silver, costly stones, wood, hay, or stubble;
each man’s work will be revealed. For the Day will declare it, because it is revealed in fire; and the fire itself will test what sort of work each man’s work is.
If any man’s work remains which he built on it, he will receive a reward.
If any man’s work is burned, he will suffer loss, but he himself will be saved, but as through fire.
Don’t you know that you are a temple of God, and that God’s Spirit lives in you?
If anyone destroys God’s temple, God will destroy him; for God’s temple is holy, which you are.
Let no one deceive himself. If anyone thinks that he is wise among you in this world, let him become a fool, that he may become wise.
For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God. For it is written, “He has taken the wise in their craftiness.”
And again, “The Lord knows the reasoning of the wise, that it is worthless.”
Therefore let no one boast in men. For all things are yours,
whether Paul, or Apollos, or Cephas, or the world, or life, or death, or things present, or things to come. All are yours,
and you are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s.

footnotes.content: Paul speaks plainly: you are still babies, not yet ready for the meat of faith. He speaks this way not to shame them, but because they are still stumbling over the most basic truths—divided loyalties, jealousy, the signs of spiritual infancy. I've watched this too: how pride mistakes comfort for maturity.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Milk is not a lesser thing; it's what the young need. But notice Paul's gentle sorrow: "not even now are you ready." Some walk with Christ for years and never move past the bottle, their hearts still turning backward when the going gets hard. Growth is not guaranteed by time alone.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jealousy and strife are the language of the flesh, the old life before grace. You can tell a church is still young in faith when its people squabble over leaders instead of looking to Jesus. The proof of spiritual growth is not eloquence or status, but the ability to love those who differ from you.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "I follow Paul" or "I follow Apollos"—the worst tragedy is turning servants of Christ into idols. Each leader is only a tool the Lord used for a season, and the moment we cling to a man instead of Jesus, we have slipped back into the flesh. Loyalty to Christ first breaks all other rivalries.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Servants through whom you believed"—a beautiful answer to the question, who are these men? Not lords, not sources of life, but vessels through which God worked. Each one given only what the Lord saw fit. Here is the corrective to every bit of celebrity that creeps into the faith: we are all servants, nothing more.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The image stays with me: I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the increase. Work has its place—steady, faithful labor—but no human work can make anything grow. We are not the power; we are the tools. This should humble us and lift a great weight off our shoulders.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters"—a hard saying for proud hearts. From the vantage of my years, I see how the Lord has been patient with my illusions of importance, gently showing me how small my work truly is beside His. Relief comes when we stop trying to be something.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Here is grace: different labors, different rewards, but all valued by the same Lord. The quiet faithful servant receives what the flashy one does not, and the flashy servant receives what he earned, no more. Each man's work will be reckoned not by applause but by the Lord's eye alone.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "God's fellow workers"—what a calling. You are not God's possessions to be idle; you are His partners in the work. At the same time, "God's farming, God's building" reminds us we belong to Him first. This tension holds us: we work hard because we belong to Him, not to ourselves or our ambitions.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul the "wise master builder" laid a foundation—a concrete image in Corinth, a city of builders. But the warning cuts deep: "let each man be careful how he builds on it." Not all construction is good construction; the materials matter, the integrity matters. The Lord sees what we cannot see.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jesus Christ is the only foundation. Everything else we attempt to build on—our own wisdom, the approval of men, earthly success—will crumble. This is the anchor sentence Paul keeps returning to. All of Corinthian pride and division rests on a lie: that something else could hold up the weight.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gold and silver endure; wood, hay, and stubble burn. The metaphor is practical and harsh. On the foundation of Christ, you can build with materials of eternal worth—love, truth, holiness—or with rubbish that only passes the moment. What are you building today? Your work will be tested.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "The Day will declare it." We cannot see now what will endure and what will burn. The Lord's fire tests our works, not our worth—we are already His. But oh, the mercy in this: the fire separates the dross from the gold. What survives will be gloriously real.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "He will receive a reward." Not that we work for wages, but the Lord does not forget faithfulness. The faithful servant, the hidden prayer, the steadfast love—these build with materials that cannot burn. This is why the humblest among us may shine brightest in the end.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Loss and yet salvation—the tender mercy here stops my heart. Even if our work is burned away, if our foundation is Christ, we pass through the fire and emerge saved. "But as through fire," stripped of all we built, seeing it was rubble all along. What grace that the builder is never destroyed.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: You are a temple—not going to be, but are right now. God's Spirit lives in you. This is the pivot from the church's divided house to each believer's holy dwelling. Your body, your mind, your will—these are the shrine where the Holy One has come to rest. Do you believe it?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The warning is severe: to destroy this temple—through willful sin, through leading others astray—is to invite destruction. Not because God is harsh, but because you cannot mock the holiness that dwells in you without consequence. The seriousness of the Christian life rests on this: He lives in me.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Let no one deceive himself." How often I have done this—dressed up my pride as conviction, my fear as wisdom, my stubbornness as faith. To become a fool in this world's eyes is to stop pretending and to let Christ remake you. The hardest step is admitting you don't have it all figured out.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "The wisdom of this world is foolishness with God." Paul quotes Job 5:13—the wise are taken in their own schemes. Every clever human system, every philosophy that leaves out the Cross, every proud reasoning that has no room for grace: these are folly in God's reckoning. Wisdom begins by bowing low.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "The Lord knows the reasoning of the wise, that it is worthless"—another quotation (Psalm 94:11). The Lord sees through every argument we craft to justify ourselves. He is not fooled by our logic or impressed by our credentials. Yet He calls us anyway, and loves us still.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Let no one boast in men." Stop leaning on human authority, human wisdom, human strength. All you need belongs to you already in Christ. This is the freedom of the gospel: you need not court favor or trade your dignity for approval. Everything is yours.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul, Apollos, Cephas—all yours. The world, life, death, present and future—all yours. Do you hear the astounding reversal? These things you thought owned you, that made you afraid or proud: they are now your servants because you belong to Christ. This is the riches of faith.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo in this verse: "You are Christ's, and Christ is God's." In a world that tells us to claim ourselves, to own ourselves, to be self-made, here stands the countercultural joy of belonging—not by accident, but by purchase and love. As of 2026-10, I am learning still that having nothing means having everything.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
